g.text: The largest dataset needs the least machinery
60 PB of map tiles is a CDN problem, not a database problem - and the routing graph everybody assumes is the hard part fits in RAM.
Three genuinely different problems wearing one product - opposite on every axis
map rendering
navigation
location updates
read or write
READ-ONLY
read-only
WRITE-ONLY on the hot path
data volume
~60 PB
~10 GB
1 TB+ / day
data mutability
near-static
slowly changing
append-only
latency need
tens of ms
seconds tolerable
fire-and-forget
the right answer
A CDN
an in-memory graph search
a write-optimized log
Almost every design mistake here comes from treating them as one system. So the design is really three designs that share a
client - and the interesting engineering is in noticing which one needs what.
A factor of six million, pointing the opposite way from everyone's intuition
map tiles
~60 PB - 5.86 x 10^12 tiles across zoom 0-21
routing graph
~10 GB - 50M intersections, 100M road segments at ~100 bytes/edge
The dataset people assume is the hard part - routing - fits in a single machine's RAM. The dataset nobody thinks about needs a
global CDN. That inversion is the single most useful thing to establish early, and it explains why the two subsystems look
nothing alike.
(21, 300001, 400000) -+-> hash 3f8a... -> ONE stored object ('empty ocean')
And the 60 PB compresses enormously, because most of the Earth is ocean, desert,
ice or unbroken forest - vast regions where adjacent high-zoom tiles are
BYTE-IDENTICAL. Store one blue tile and reference it billions of times, and real
storage drops by orders of magnitude.
Recognising that the naive 60 PB is a CEILING rather than an estimate is the
useful move; quoting it as the answer is not.
694,000 GPS samples/sec - and the fix is a battery decision that happens to also be a capacity one
1B DAU x 35 min/week / 7 = 5 billion navigation-minutes/day. A sample every 5 seconds = 6 x 10^10 samples/day.
1 sample / request
10 samples / request
15 samples / request
Batching 15 samples - 75 seconds of movement - cuts request volume 15x. But the number that matters is not requests/sec: on a
phone it is the difference between the cellular radio being CONTINUOUSLY AWAKE and waking briefly once a minute. ON MOBILE THE
RADIO IS USUALLY THE LARGEST SINGLE CONSUMER OF BATTERY, so this serves the 'data and battery frugality' requirement, and the
capacity saving is a side effect. History is ~40 bytes per sample = 2.4 TB/day, append-only, retained for traffic modelling.
Three subsystems, deliberately barely coupled
1 rendering: precompute everything, serve it from a CDN
Tiles are IMMUTABLE and their URL is COMPUTABLE from the
client's position and zoom - so the client needs no API call
to know what to fetch, and every tile is cacheable forever at
the edge. That is what turns 60 PB into a static-asset
problem, and why the largest dataset needs the least
infrastructure.
2 navigation: apply tiling to the GRAPH too
The road graph is small in bytes, but a shortest-path search
over 100 million edges is far too slow interactively. So the
graph is cut into ROUTING TILES - subgraphs with references to
their neighbours - and the search loads only the tiles it
traverses. Crucially they exist at MULTIPLE LEVELS OF DETAIL:
a cross-country route uses coarse motorway-only tiles and
switches to fine-grained ones near the endpoints.
3 location: fire-and-forget, then stream it
Batched samples land in Cassandra for history and Kafka for
real-time consumers. Traffic conditions are derived from the
aggregate and fed back into routing-tile edge weights. And the
client's own position is NEVER READ BACK from the server - the
phone already knows where it is.
The elegant part: THE SAME TILING IDEA SOLVES TWO OF THE THREE PROBLEMS, for two different reasons. Map tiles exist so the
client downloads only what it can SEE; routing tiles exist so the search algorithm loads only what it TRAVERSES. Same
technique, different motivation - and recognising the reuse is what makes the design feel coherent rather than like three
unrelated systems.
Two map concepts that carry real design weight
a degree of latitude is ~111 km everywhere. A degree of longitude is not.
Longitude shrinks from 111 km at the equator to ZERO at the poles. So a naive bounding box of +/-0.01 degrees is a square in
Kenya and a tall thin rectangle in Norway - which is why distance filtering needs the haversine formula rather than coordinate
arithmetic. The asymmetry is the reason, not a detail.
Web Mercator preserves local SHAPE and angles, and wildly distorts AREA
Flattening a sphere always distorts something - area, shape, distance or direction - and you cannot preserve all four. Web
Mercator keeps roads meeting at the correct angles (so the map looks right when you zoom in) at the cost of Greenland looking
the size of Africa. Correct for a navigation product: nobody navigates by comparing the areas of countries, and everybody
navigates by following the shape of a junction.
Three API details that carry real weight
202 Accepted, not 200 OK, for location updates
the server has taken the batch and will process it
asynchronously; it makes no promise the samples were
stored. The honest status code for a fire-and-forget
write, and it lets the ingest path acknowledge before
touching Cassandra or Kafka.
the polyline is an ENCODED STRING, not an array
a cross-country route has thousands of points; as JSON
that is hundreds of kilobytes. Encoded polyline stores
successive DELTAS in a variable-length encoding,
typically cutting the payload 8-10x - the
battery-and-data requirement showing up somewhere
unexpected.
tile URLs are computed CLIENT-SIDE from (z, x, y)
no round trip to ask 'which tiles do I need' - the
tiling scheme is a CONVENTION both sides know. The
cost: that convention is then extremely hard to
change, because old clients keep computing old URLs
for years.
